newsitem.title: MEXICO: Protests mount as Mexican faces U.S. execution.
newsitem.headline: Protests mount as Mexican faces U.S. execution.

text.p: About 400 Mexicans blocked a border bridge seperating Mexico from the United States on Wednesday in a last-minute bid to prevent the execution in Texas of countryman Irineo Tristan Montoya.
As the U.S. Supreme Court rejected a final appeal for the 30-year-old Mexican, angry family members and supporters at the bridge clamoured desperately for his life.
"Now things are really stacked against us. We don't have anything against anybody but we're desperate," Dario Tristan, brother of the condemned man, told Reuters, tears welling up in his eyes.

Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria sent a letter early on Wednesday to Texas Gov. George Bush, urging him to stay the execution of Irineo Tristan Montoya on humanitarian grounds for 30 days, while a final investigation into the case is carried out.
But speaking to reporters at the Caribbean beach resort of Cancun later Wednesday, he indicated there was little left the government could do.
The condemned man's mother, Emilia Montoya, herself dying of lung cancer, also made an appeal to Bush, the only person left who could save her son's life.
"May God touch the heart of Governor Bush," she told Formato 21 radio in Mexico. "The life of my son is in his hands."

Her husband, Honourio Tristan, appealed to Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo to step in, a call that was echoed on the Matamoros bridge by some of the supporters, who held up banners urging Zedillo to persuade the U.S. government to grant an 11th-hour clemency.
The execution, scheduled for 6 p.m. CDT (2300 GMT) in Hunstville, Texas, has caused an uproar in Mexico, where the death penalty is banned and considered cruel and inhuman.
As Mexicans protested, Tristan bid farewell to his parents at the Texas jail where he is scheduled to die.
He was not granted his last wish of hugging his sick mother before he died.

Tristan, convicted of stabbing to death a motorist in 1985, remained calm during the farewell visit by his parents and said he would remain that way to the end, Mexico's consul-general in Houston, Manuel Perez Cardenas, who witnessed the visit, told Televisa television network.

"He didn't shed a tear. He hasn't lost his strength, his emotional equilibrium, for a single moment and his optimism is still alive," he said, before the appeal was rejected by the U.S. Supreme Court.
The scheduled execution has sent shudders through the national psyche, particularly as many Mexicans feel the U.S. justice system is biased against Mexican immigrants.
There are some 35 Mexicans on U.S. death row. Only four Mexicans have been executed, however, in the last 50 years, according to state news agency Notimex.
